hook: News reports say "cases are still rising, but more slowly." That sentence is about concavity: the count is increasing, but its rate of increase is falling. The moment the rate stops speeding up and starts slowing down is a point of inflection, and it is often the most watched point on a graph.

ideas: Concave up on an interval: $f'$ is increasing there ($f'' > 0$). Concave down: $f'$ is decreasing ($f'' < 0$).
Point of inflection: a point on the graph where the concavity changes, that is, where $f''$ changes sign, or where $f'$ changes from increasing to decreasing or back.
On a graph of $f'$: inflection points of $f$ are at the high and low points of $f'$, not at its zeros.
Candidates are where $f'' = 0$ or $f''$ does not exist; then check the sign of $f''$ on each side.

misconception.wrong: $f''(c) = 0$, so the graph of $f$ has a point of inflection at $x = c$.
misconception.right: $f''(c) = 0$ only makes $c$ a candidate. The concavity must actually change: $f''$ must change sign. $f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ but is concave up on both sides. On a graph of $f'$, also do not confuse zeros of $f'$ (extrema of $f$) with turns of $f'$ (inflection points).

summary: The sign of $f''$ gives the concavity: $f'' > 0$ (equivalently $f'$ increasing) means concave up, $f'' < 0$ means concave down. A point of inflection is where the concavity changes, so $f''$ must change sign; $f''(c) = 0$ alone is not enough. On a graph of $f'$, look at where $f'$ turns.
